[quote=averne;60078511][b]The Road to the Empire: March  December 2025[/b]
[i]Albany, Hither, and Averne, before the Acts of Union[/i][/quote]

[b]2025  March to June: The First Sparks[/b]
It all began in March, which felt appropriately dramatic. The Ides of March, the wags called it, after King Erjk Drs of Thýven sent his emissaries across the strait with the audacious proposal of a [i]crown-union[/i]. On paper, it was madness: three fractious Commonwealths across the peninsula were barely able to tolerate one another, let alone bind themselves to a northern monarchy.

The official response in Albanys legislature was predictable. First, they laughed. Then they mocked. Then the Federalists stood up to deliver fiery speeches about sovereignty while their Unionist rivals jeered from the benches. Meanwhile, Averne and Hither tried not to choke on their wine at the idea of binding their fates to a foreign crown while they hadnt even solved their own.

But under the laughter came unease. By April, the economy was wheezing. Overlapping tax codes, rival social programs, three different armies consuming three different budgetsit was a recipe for financial collapse. Creditors warned of a possible liquidity crisis by autumn. The Magnates League circulated private memos with lines like, without systemic reform, expect full market contraction within the year. In polite English: the money was about to die.

That April, the treasury departments were juggling deficits of nearly 12% of GDP across all three states, and central banks had begun issuing contradictory policies: Albany cut interest rates while Averne raised them, and Hither floated its currency outright. Investors called it monetary suicide by committee.

The people felt it, too. Albic merchants groaned under redundant tariffs. Hinterland farmers protested low subsidies. Avernic shipping magnates panicked about shrinking foreign contracts. Even the clergy began to mutter. Preachers in the Highlands spoke of divine punishment for disunity, while coastal guilds held mass prayers for stability.

By June, nostalgia took the stage. Newspapers began to romanticize the [i]Old Empire[/i]. Was it glorious? Stable? A disaster wrapped in marble? All of the above. The only fact that mattered was that people remembered it. Editorials reprinted centuries-old paintings of emperors beneath the [i]White Tree[/i]. Academics published florid essays about how the Albic, Avernic, and Hinterlander peoples were always one. And suddenly, the Old Idea was back.

Nostalgia was not limited to the press. Schoolchildren in Albany were suddenly taught poems about the Tree City. In Averne, theater companies staged overwrought plays of emperors long dead. In Hither, old ballads of unification were sung in taverns. What had been dusty footnotes in libraries became living propaganda, and the people swallowed it eagerly.

[b]2025  July to September: The Stirring of the Old Crown[/b]
Summer was chaos wrapped in conspiracy.

Parties hardened into trenches. The [i]Unionists[/i] shouted that reform was the only way to prevent apocalypse. The [i]Federalists[/i] countered that sovereignty was sacredtranslation: their careers depended on it. Meanwhile, fringe monarchists crawled out of the woodwork, each brandishing a different genealogy of some lost imperial house.

The military was subtler. Generals with Albic bloodlines called their Hinterland classmates. Admirals with Avernic ties called up coastal magnates. Old boys networks, forged in academies decades before, began threading quiet promises: no civil war, no coups, no juntas. The officer corps agreedthey would not destroy the Commonwealths to save them.

Some officers spoke more plainly. General Fornan of Albany warned that if unity is not chosen, civil war will be chosen for us. Admiral Arvek of Averne told colleagues that the navy would not fire on fellow Vespurians under any circumstance. The Hither militias, notoriously independent, quietly reassured the Crown emissaries that they would not oppose union if it came  so long as their land rights were preserved.

And all the while, the Magnates kept meeting behind oak doors, chain-smoking and muttering, Imperial Reform, Imperial Reform.

By late August, the word itself returned: Empire. Hithers ran full-page columns titled The Law of the Crown. Rural preachers thundered from pulpits. The aristocracy polished dusty crests. In Albany, a young deputy called the Empire our last firewall before ruin, and to the horror of his party, the press cheered.

[b]2025  October: The Summit of Pretenders[/b]
October was when things turned surreal.

Myst Isle hosted a grand summit: nobles, clerics, magnates, and party chiefs all crammed together. The purpose? To decide who, if anyone, might wear a crown. The result? Chaos. At least a hundred dozen claimants appearedancient dynasties, self-proclaimed heirs, paper kings, fanatics, and charlatans. Each had baggage, ambition, or toxic patronage. Every candidate was poison.

And then, casually, a name surfaced: [i]Lux[/i].

Governor of Myst Isle. Veteran of the frontier campaigns. Moderate senator. Old family, respected but not overbearing. A man of steel, but not ambition. In fact, the only man who hadnt asked for the throne. And for that reason, he became the only man fit for it.

The elites seized on him. Nobles whispered compromise. Clerics muttered divine providence. The Magnates nodded approvingly. Even the Federalists didnt object too strongly, because Lux wasnt one of those lunatic dynasts.

The irony? Lux had no idea.

In reality, Lux spent most of October fretting about road repairs on Myst Isle, and attending the county harvest festival where he judged a pumpkin competition. He wrote in his diary that he might angle for the Ministry of Agriculture if the Unionists gained control. When he returned to his office, three bishops, two magnates, and a half-dozen generals had already written his coronation speech. He just drank some Pepsi and resumed his 3rd day of his rewatch of LOTR: Extended edition before going to bed after dinner with his wife and children.

[b]2025  November: The People Move[/b]
By November, the whisper campaign had bloomed into rallies.

Farmers in Hither marched under banners reading One Crown, One People. Dockworkers in Albany lit torches and paraded through the streets. Avernic merchants rallied on the wharves, chanting for stability. Half of it was spontaneous. Half was encouraged by Magnate funding and subtle party organizing. The press latched on: The Crown Returns ran in headlines across the Commonwealths.

Polls confirmed it: over 70% of the public now supported some form of Union. The Federalists began to panic. The Unionists smelled blood. The nobility saw opportunity.

And Lux? Still clueless. In his senate office, he joked that maybe hed finally get that cabinet post. Outside his door, magnates, generals, and clerics were already stitching his coronation robe.

The legislatures, cornered by public opinion and economic panic, convened in late November. The debates were brutal: the Federalists screamed of tyranny, the Unionists shouted back with collapse charts. Finally, the vote came down.

In Albany, the Unionists carried the vote by a hair: 183 to 171. Hithers legislature fell in line 94 to 82, with Hinterland agrarians abstaining en masse. Averne passed the motion 201 to 190, after shipping magnates flipped under Magnate League pressure. Every roll-call revealed the same pattern: one side screaming collapse, the other screaming tyranny, and both sides looking like they were watching the abyss open.

All three legislatures passed motions for unionand all three assemblies, with suspicious synchronicity, declared [i]Lux[/i] as the chosen Emperor.

Minus one vote: his own.

He protested, demanded at least a universal ballot. The assemblies agreedthinking it would fail. Instead, the referendum returned overwhelming numbers: 72% Yes, 24% abstain, 3% No. A done deal. Lux was Emperor.

The absurdity wasnt lost on anyone. From the outside, it looked like madness. From the inside, it was pure inevitability: every lobby, every faction, every clique had spent six months running around like the apocalypse was tomorrow. By the time Luxs name was drawn, the machine was already built. He didnt climb onto the throne. The throne was shoved under him.

[b]2025  December: Hyperion and the White Tree[/b]

December was madness.

The legislatures of Albany, Hither, and Averne voted narrowlybut decisivelyfor Union. The question of a capital tore open old wounds. Albany, Averne, Hitherall demanded it. The next question was: [i]where?[/i]

The answer was instant and horrifying: [b]The Old Capital.[/b]

To archaeologists, it was a nightmare. The ruins were the oldest on the continent: once a tribal encampment, then a marketplace, then a city of marble and dynasties, fourteen in total, six of them imperial. The White TreeA living god of wood and leaf. Five thousand meters tall, two hundred wide, white bark gleaming with gold-veined leaves. Worshiped by tribes before settlers, revered by kings after them. Visible from the shores, from the heavens themselves. Untouched by time, plague, famine, or war. The symbol of Empirehad been sacred for millennia. The city had been abandoned centuries ago, left to archeologists, theologians, a handful of locals, and security detachments.

It had been called the Whitestone City, the Tree City, the Last True Capital. Its walls had never fallen by siege, only by betrayal or famine. Now, it was to be resurrected in one winter. The name chosen: [b]Hyperion[/b], Eternal Light.

By mid-December, tens of thousands flocked to the ruins. Immigration was instant, people claiming land inside half-intact walls. Builders, priests, magnates, guildsmen. Within weeks, the ruins swarmed with cranes and scaffolding. The White Tree, visible from orbit, stood watch. Airspace was locked down. Military patrols encircled the city. Archeologists screamed, but the Crown decreed: the Capital lives again.

Surveyors rushed in first, mapping collapsed streets. Engineers argued how to rebuild sewers last used centuries ago. Soldiers strung barbed wire around the White Tree while priests begged them not to. Thousands of settlers swarmed ahead of them all, hammering down tents inside ancient marble courtyards, staking claims to crumbling mansions with nothing but chalk and rope. Hyperion was chaos, but chaos with purpose.

Whole families camped inside roofless palaces, scrawling property of the Crown on ancient marble with spray paint. Merchants opened stalls beneath broken colonnades. Priests built shrines in collapsed auditoriums. Even taverns popped up under the Trees shadow, serving ale in clay cups stamped First in Hyperion.

The chaos of Hyperions rebirth nearly broke the dream before it began. Families claimed ancient mansions with tents and rifles; guilds staked courtyards with banners; priests and archaeologists brawled over shrines. To prevent bloodshed, the Crown issued the [i]Hyperion Charter[/i]: no private claims would be honored without registration, every citizen was entitled to a plot, and ancient ruins would be preserved as national monuments. Within weeks, surveyors demarcated new neighborhoodsNew Marble, Tree Quarter, Riversidewhile scaffolds rose alongside temples older than memory. It was neither purely old nor entirely new; Hyperion became both, a city reborn by compromise.

[b]End of 2025  Consolidation of the Union[/b]
The Hyperian Constitution was proclaimed at midnight on the winter solstice. Monarchy bound to federal democracy. Nobles tied to administrative offices. Governors kept autonomy but bowed to central law. The military centralized, diplomacy unified, currency standardized.

Minorities were explicitly guaranteed rights: Elves and Dwarves cultural autonomy, Bestials military integration, Magi regulated but honored, even the undead offered recognition under law. For the Magnates, markets stabilized. For the military, budgets saved. For politicians, stability without tyranny. For the people, the dream restored.

The economic turnaround was immediate and stunning. By January, merged tax codes saved billions in duplicated bureaucracy. A unified tariff system ended months of strangling trade disputes. Albanys banks, Avernes shipping houses, and Hithers granaries were suddenly bound by one market, one currency, one fiscal code. Credit flowed again, wages rose, and unemployment dipped within weeks. Newspapers printed charts showing a vertical rebound: Imperial Stability = Prosperity. The very crisis that had nearly doomed them was now the proof that Union was salvation.

Luxnow [b]Emperor Aurean I of Vespuria[/b]stood bewildered. His family, expecting perhaps a cabinet post, were now Imperial. The White Tree rose over Hyperion. The Empire was back.

The Lux family itself had to be remade overnight. His wife, once content as a Myst Isle society matron, was suddenly styled Empress, thrust into endless parades and ceremonies she had never rehearsed for. His children, who until then had argued about boarding schools and university placements, found themselves under tutors in etiquette and genealogy, schooled in dynasties they had never expected to join. To ordinary citizens, this ordinariness was precisely the charm: unlike the overbearing dynasts of old, the Lux family had never asked for crowns, and so the people were eager to grant them one.

[quote=averne;60078511][i]Thus, by the end of 2025, the Three Commonwealths had become One Crown. The old dream lived again, and Hyperion once more burned bright on the map of the world.[/i][/quote]

[i]Then someone remembered Thývens proposal. It was accepted quietly, because the truth was embarrassing: unification had narrowly prevented an economic collapse on the scale of 1920. Now it was Two Empires, Two Thrones, Two Crowns, Two Emperors. Twice as Great. Twice as absurd. And yet, entirely real.

[sub]Arean was quietly sobbing in his new office as he signed the [b]Act of Union[/b] with the Northerners; he just wanted to watch the Extended Edition in peace after work.[/sub][/i]
[/spoiler]

[b]The Union of the Strong Part 2[/b]
[i]August 2025[/i]
The reaction to the commission's report was explosive needless to say, the Fondenfoddel found themselves quickly divided over the minutiae of the commission's secret actions over the past decade, quietly moving in the shadows of the governments of the states across the sea and Thýven, some argued it was government and royal overreach, others argued the sanctity of the monarchy, no one one the debates. In the meantime the general public found the commission to be long and tedious, economists were amused, and nationalists were for the first time ever divided between whether it was manifest destiny or anti-nationalist to even consider the union. 

As the month continued the eyes of the diplomats and government officials in Thýven turned amusedly to the events in the lands across the strait, the fever of unification had stirred in the bones of the three disjointed states, while a few people speculated that this was the result of the commission, those who knew, knew that the unification push amongst the three states was not related to the commission.

[i]November 2025[/i]

While the month of September had gone without much issue, the stirrings of nationalism and unification in the south had become hard to ignore, nor were the stirrings of imperialism within the monarchy. It didnt help that the monarch had recently filled the vacant caliphate of Sal-Baliz with his own self and declared himself a caliph of a new caliphate, a move which while contested in court, was permitted on the grounds of ceremony. 

The win in the courts had led to a further vigorous reaction from the nationalists in the legislature, who had now grown greatly in size since the September mid-terms, which had seen the Fondenfoddel lean farther right than usual, primarily due to fearmongering from the economists and military strategists and companies that backed the legislature. It was thus that the debate over whether the lands of Thýven now constituted in size enough to formally grant the title of Emperor to the king. This matter was quickly seized upon by the media who attempted to frame this as a royal takeover, however, in a surprising move Erjk Drs politely declined the overly stuffy title, though in reality the royal offices were already moving to change the titles and names in the background.
